title: Second Temple to Yavneh
bigQuestion: How did a people whose Temple was destroyed turn a small town of scholars into the seed of the Talmud?

story.title: Give Me Yavneh
story.kicker: A rabbi leaves a city under siege inside a coffin, and asks a general for a town instead of a treasure.
paragraphs: The year is 70 CE. Roman soldiers ring the walls of Jerusalem. Inside, food is running out, and armed groups of Jews fight each other about whether to surrender. An old teacher named Yochanan ben Zakkai wants to get out. The gates are guarded. The rebels kill anyone who tries to leave.

The Talmud, in tractate Gittin (page 56), tells what happened next. Yochanan's students spread the word that their teacher has died. They carry him out through the gate in a coffin. The guards let a funeral pass. Outside the walls, the teacher climbs out, alive, and asks to see the Roman commander, Vespasian.

Vespasian, the story says, is about to become emperor. He tells the rabbi he may ask for one thing. Yochanan does not ask for the Temple. He does not ask for gold or for his own safety. He says, in the words the Gemara gives him: Give me Yavneh and its sages. Yavneh is a small town near the coast. Its sages are the teachers who study there.

Later rabbis wondered about that choice. Some in the Gemara ask whether he should have asked for Jerusalem itself. Historians point out that the story was written down long after the event, and that no Roman source mentions it. But everyone agrees on what came after. Within a few years, Yavneh was a center of study, and the Temple lay in ruins.

This chapter follows the road to that moment: Judea under Greek and Roman rule, the groups who argued over how to be Jewish, the teachers Hillel and Shammai, the war, and the town where Jewish learning started over. It ends with a second war, a rabbi who died reciting the Shema, and a book called the Mishnah.
story.think: Yochanan asked for a town of scholars, not for the Temple or the city. What do you think he believed that choice would protect?

lessons.title: Greek Kings, Then Rome
lessons.mainIdea: For three centuries before the Talmud's rabbis, Judea lived under Greek-speaking kings and then under Rome.
reading: In 332 BCE Alexander the Great marched through the region historians call Judea, the land around Jerusalem. After his death, Greek-speaking kings ruled it, first from Egypt and then from Syria. Greek became the language of trade and government. Many Jews learned it. Some also took Greek names and customs.

In 167 BCE the Syrian king Antiochus IV outlawed Jewish practice and put a foreign altar in the *Temple* in Jerusalem. A family of priests, the Maccabees, led a revolt. By 164 BCE they had retaken the Temple. Jewish tradition remembers that moment each year at Hanukkah. For about a century, Judea had its own kings.

Then Rome arrived. In 63 BCE the Roman general Pompey entered Jerusalem. From that point Judea was under Roman power, sometimes through a local king like Herod, sometimes through a Roman governor. Rome collected taxes and kept soldiers in the land. This is the world in which the first rabbis of the Talmud lived.

words.d: the land around Jerusalem in the Second Temple period; the Roman name for the province
the house of worship in Jerusalem where priests offered sacrifices; the Second Temple stood from c. 516 BCE to 70 CE
the family of priests who led a revolt against the Syrian Greek king in 167 BCE and retook the Temple

look.title: Rulers of Judea, in Order
look.cite: Dates as commonly given by historians; see Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, books 11–15 (1st century CE)
look.prompt: Put the four powers in order: Greek kings, Maccabees, Rome, Herod under Rome. About how many years passed between the first and the last?

check.q: Who entered Jerusalem in 63 BCE and began Roman control of Judea?
check.why: Pompey, a Roman general, entered Jerusalem in 63 BCE. Alexander came in 332 BCE, and Antiochus was a Syrian Greek king.

check.q: What did the Maccabees do in 164 BCE?
choices: Retook the Temple from Antiochus IV
check.why: The Maccabean revolt retook the Temple in 164 BCE, a moment Jewish tradition remembers at Hanukkah.

check.q: Which language became common for trade and government in Judea after Alexander?
check.why: Greek-speaking kings ruled after Alexander, so Greek spread in trade and government.

lessons.title: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes
lessons.mainIdea: Jews in the Second Temple period belonged to different groups, and the rabbis of the Talmud grew out of the Pharisees.
reading: The Jewish historian Josephus, writing in the 1st century CE, describes three main groups among the Jews of his day. He calls them the *Pharisees*, the *Sadducees* and the *Essenes*. They agreed on the Torah. They disagreed about how to read it, who should lead, and what happens after death.

The Pharisees, Josephus says, followed traditions handed down from their teachers alongside the written Torah. Rabbinic tradition later called those traditions the Oral Torah and traced the rabbis back to the Pharisees. The Sadducees were linked to the priests and the Temple. They accepted the written Torah and rejected the Pharisees' added traditions. The Mishnah records arguments between the two groups.

The *Essenes* lived in tight communities, shared property and kept strict rules of purity. In 1947 shepherds found ancient scrolls in caves near Qumran by the Dead Sea. Many scholars think the people who kept those scrolls were Essenes or a group like them, though this is still debated.

When the Temple fell in 70 CE, the Sadducees lost their center, and the Essene communities disappear from the record. The Pharisees' way of study survived. The Talmud does not use the word Pharisee often; it speaks of sages. But historians see a clear line from the Pharisees to the rabbis.

words.d: a Jewish group of the Second Temple period that followed handed-down traditions along with the written Torah; the rabbis' forerunners
a Jewish group tied to the priests and the Temple that accepted the written Torah but not the Pharisees' traditions
a Jewish group that lived in strict, close communities; many scholars link them to the Dead Sea Scrolls

look.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls in Numbers
rows: Year the first scrolls were found
Copies of Isaiah among them, about
look.cite: Commonly cited figures from the Israel Antiquities Authority and standard scroll surveys
look.prompt: Why might finding many copies of Isaiah in one library tell us something about what that community valued?

check.q: Which group do historians see as the forerunners of the rabbis?
check.why: The Pharisees followed handed-down traditions alongside the written Torah, and historians trace the rabbis to them.

check.q: Who wrote the 1st-century description of the three Jewish groups?
check.why: Josephus, a Jewish historian writing in the 1st century CE, describes the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes.

check.q: Which group was most closely tied to the priests and the Temple?
check.why: Josephus and the Mishnah link the Sadducees to the priests and the Temple.

lessons.title: Hillel and Shammai
lessons.mainIdea: Hillel and Shammai, teachers of about the 1st century BCE, gave the Talmud its first great pair of disagreeing schools.
reading: Two teachers stand at the start of nearly every list of rabbis: *Hillel* and *Shammai*. Tradition places them in Jerusalem in about the 1st century BCE, in the days of King Herod. Hillel, tradition says, came from Babylon and was poor. Shammai was a builder. Each had students, and the students formed two schools, the House of Hillel and the House of Shammai.

The Mishnah records more than three hundred disagreements between the two houses. The House of Shammai often read a rule strictly. The House of Hillel often read it more leniently. The Gemara in tractate Eruvin (page 13) says a heavenly voice declared that both are the words of the living God, but that the law follows the House of Hillel, because they were humble and taught the other side's view first.

The best-known Hillel story is in tractate Shabbat (page 31). A stranger asks to be taught the whole Torah while standing on one foot. Shammai sends him away. Hillel answers: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow; that is the whole Torah, the rest is explanation, go and learn. In *Pirkei Avot* (1:14) Hillel asks: if I am not for myself, who will be for me? And if I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when?

words.d: a teacher in Jerusalem of about the 1st century BCE, known for patience and lenient rulings; founder of the House of Hillel
Hillel's contemporary, known for strict rulings; founder of the House of Shammai
Chapters of the Fathers, a tractate of the Mishnah made of sayings by the sages rather than laws

look.title: Hillel's Three Questions
look.text: Hillel used to say: If I am not for myself, who will be for me? And when I am for myself alone, what am I? And if not now, when?
look.cite: Mishnah Avot 1:14, paraphrased from Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers (1877)
look.prompt: The three questions pull in different directions: care for yourself, care for others, act now. How do they fit together?

check.q: According to Eruvin 13b, why does the law follow the House of Hillel?
choices: They were humble and taught the other view first
check.why: The Gemara says the House of Hillel was humble and taught the House of Shammai's opinion before its own.

check.q: What did Hillel tell the stranger who asked to learn the Torah on one foot?
choices: What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow
check.why: In Shabbat 31a Hillel gives that rule, calls the rest explanation, and sends the man to study.

check.q: Where are the sayings of Hillel like 'If not now, when?' found?
check.why: Pirkei Avot, a tractate of the Mishnah, collects sayings of the sages; Hillel's is at Avot 1:14.

lessons.title: The War With Rome, 66–70 CE
lessons.mainIdea: A revolt against Rome ended with the burning of the Second Temple in 70 CE, the turning point of Jewish history that the Talmud's rabbis lived after.
reading: In 66 CE Jews in Judea rose against Roman rule. High taxes, cruel governors and clashes between Jews and Greeks in the cities all fed the anger. Rome sent its general Vespasian with legions. When Vespasian became emperor in 69, his son Titus took over the war. In the spring of 70, Titus laid *siege* to Jerusalem.

Josephus, who first fought against Rome and then surrendered and joined the Roman side, wrote the fullest account in his book The Jewish War. He describes hunger inside the walls, fighting between Jewish factions, and the fire that destroyed the Temple in the summer of 70. Jewish tradition marks that day as the ninth of the month of Av and fasts on it.

In Rome the emperor's family built a stone arch to celebrate. The Arch of Titus still stands, and its carving shows soldiers carrying the Temple's menorah, the seven-branched lamp, through the streets of Rome. For historians it is one of the clearest pieces of evidence for the event.

The Talmud tells the war differently, as a lesson. In tractate Gittin (pages 55–56) the Gemara says Jerusalem fell because of a dinner party gone wrong: a host embarrassed a guest named Bar Kamtza in front of the sages, and no one stopped him. The rabbis read the disaster as a warning about *baseless hatred* among Jews, not only about Roman armies.

words.d: surrounding a city with an army so that no one can get in or out, in order to force it to surrender
hatred with no good reason; the Gemara names it as the cause of the Second Temple's fall
a Jewish general who joined the Roman side and wrote The Jewish War and Antiquities of the Jews in the 1st century CE

look.title: Two Tellings of One Fall
look.text: Josephus, an eyewitness, says Jerusalem fell to Roman legions after a long siege, made worse by Jews fighting each other inside the walls. The Gemara in Gittin 55b–56a says Jerusalem fell because of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza: a guest was thrown out of a feast in front of the sages, and no one protested. Both tellings blame division among Jews. One asks what happened; the other asks what it should teach.
look.prompt: What can a historian learn from Josephus that the Talmud does not give? What does the Talmud offer that a battle report does not?

check.q: Who led the Roman siege of Jerusalem in 70 CE?
check.why: Titus, Vespasian's son, took over the war when his father became emperor and besieged Jerusalem in 70 CE.

check.q: What does the Arch of Titus in Rome show?
choices: The building of the Second Temple
check.why: The arch's carving shows Roman soldiers carrying the menorah taken from the Temple.

check.q: How does the Gemara in Gittin explain why Jerusalem fell?
choices: A guest was shamed at a feast and no one protested
check.why: The Kamtza and Bar Kamtza story blames baseless hatred among Jews, shown when a guest was shamed and the sages stayed silent.

lessons.title: Yochanan ben Zakkai's Escape
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbinic tradition tells that Yochanan ben Zakkai left besieged Jerusalem and won permission to teach at Yavneh, and later rabbis both honored and questioned his choice.
reading: *Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai* was, by tradition, the youngest student of Hillel and the leading sage in Jerusalem during the war. The title Rabban, our master, marks him as head of the sages. The Gemara in Gittin 56a–b tells how he had himself carried out of the city in a coffin, because the rebels let no one leave alive.

Outside the walls he greeted Vespasian as emperor. The Roman said he was not emperor. Then a messenger arrived from Rome with the news that he was. Impressed, Vespasian offered a request. Yochanan asked for Yavneh and its sages, for the family of Rabban Gamliel to be spared, and for a doctor for Rabbi Tzadok, who had fasted for years.

The Gemara does not simply praise him. It quotes Rabbi Yosef, or some say Rabbi Akiva, applying a verse to Yochanan: God turns wise men backward. He should have asked Vespasian to spare Jerusalem, the objection goes. The Gemara answers that Yochanan feared asking too much and getting nothing. This is a *sugya* about a choice, with both sides kept.

Historians note that a similar story of a Jewish leader predicting Vespasian's rise is told by Josephus about himself. They cannot confirm the coffin or the meeting. What they can see is the result: within a generation, Yavneh had a court and a school, and the sages there began reshaping Jewish life without a Temple.

words.d: the sage who, tradition says, escaped besieged Jerusalem and founded the center of study at Yavneh after 70 CE
a town near the coast of Judea where the sages gathered after the Temple's fall; Greek sources call it Jamnia
a unit of Talmud discussion on one question, with proofs, objections and answers

look.title: The Request at the Roman Camp
look.text: Vespasian said to him: I am leaving, and I will send someone else. But ask something of me, and I will give it. He said: Give me Yavneh and its sages, and the family line of Rabban Gamliel, and doctors to heal Rabbi Tzadok.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 56b, paraphrased from the Aramaic (compare the William Davidson Talmud, Sefaria, and Rodkinson's abridged edition, 1896–1903)
look.prompt: Three requests: a school, a family, a healer. What does each one protect?

check.q: How, according to Gittin 56a, did Yochanan ben Zakkai leave Jerusalem?
check.why: His students carried him out in a coffin, since the rebels allowed only the dead to pass.

check.q: What objection does the Gemara raise about Yochanan's request?
choices: He should have asked Vespasian to spare Jerusalem
He should have asked for gold
check.why: A sage in the Gemara says he should have asked for Jerusalem; the Gemara answers that he feared getting nothing at all.

check.q: What does the title Rabban mean?
choices: Our master, used for the head of the sages
check.why: Rabban, our master, was used for the leading sage, such as Yochanan ben Zakkai and the Gamliel family.

lessons.title: Prayer in Place of Sacrifice
lessons.mainIdea: After 70 CE the sages taught that prayer, study and acts of kindness could serve where sacrifices once had.
reading: For centuries Jewish worship had centered on the Temple. Priests offered animals, grain and incense on the altar each day and on festivals. Jews traveled to Jerusalem for Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot. With the Temple gone, the biggest question was practical: how does one serve God now?

A rabbinic text called *Avot de-Rabbi Natan* (chapter 4) gives Yochanan ben Zakkai's answer. Walking past the ruins with his student Rabbi Yehoshua, who mourns that the place of atonement is destroyed, Yochanan says: do not grieve, we have another atonement as good, acts of loving-kindness. He quotes the prophet Hosea: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.

The sages at Yavneh also gave prayer a fixed shape. The Gemara in Berakhot 28b says that a sage named Shimon HaPakuli arranged the eighteen blessings in order before Rabban Gamliel at Yavneh. That prayer, the *Amidah*, is still the center of Jewish daily services. Rabbinic tradition holds that its times match the times of the daily Temple offerings.

Study itself became a kind of service. The Talmud often says that one who studies the laws of the offerings is counted as if he had brought them. Historians see this shift as the birth of rabbinic Judaism: a religion of synagogue, study house and home, which could survive anywhere.

words.d: an early rabbinic commentary on Pirkei Avot with many stories about the sages
the standing prayer of eighteen (now nineteen) blessings, arranged at Yavneh, said at each daily service
making up for a wrong; in the Temple this was done with offerings, and the sages taught that kindness and prayer could also serve

look.title: Mercy, Not Sacrifice
look.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt-offerings.
look.cite: Hosea 6:6, JPS Tanakh (1917), the verse Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4 gives to Yochanan ben Zakkai
look.prompt: The verse was written centuries before the Temple fell. Why would a teacher after 70 CE reach for it?

check.q: In Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4, what does Yochanan say can serve as atonement now?
check.why: Yochanan tells Rabbi Yehoshua that acts of loving-kindness are an atonement as good, quoting Hosea 6:6.

check.q: Who, in Berakhot 28b, arranged the eighteen blessings at Yavneh?
check.why: The Gemara names Shimon HaPakuli, who set the blessings in order before Rabban Gamliel at Yavneh.

check.q: Which prophet's words are quoted: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice?
check.why: The verse is Hosea 6:6 in the JPS 1917 translation.

sections.title: Yavneh, Bar Kokhba and the Galilee

lessons.title: The Court at Yavneh
lessons.mainIdea: At Yavneh the sages under Rabban Gamliel II settled the calendar, the prayers and many disputes, and the Talmud remembers both their authority and their quarrels.
reading: After Yochanan ben Zakkai, leadership at Yavneh passed to *Rabban Gamliel II*, grandson of the Gamliel mentioned in the New Testament as Paul's teacher. The sages there acted as a court. They fixed which month the new moon began, which set the dates of every festival for Jews everywhere. They decided which of the disputed rulings of Hillel and Shammai to follow.

The Talmud shows Gamliel as a strong, sometimes harsh leader. In Rosh Hashanah 25a he orders Rabbi Yehoshua, who calculated a different date for Yom Kippur, to appear before him on that date carrying his staff and money, to show that the court's ruling stands even if it is wrong. Rabbi Yehoshua obeys. The Gemara praises his humility and the court's authority together.

In Berakhot 27b–28a the sages remove Gamliel from office after he shames Rabbi Yehoshua once too often. They appoint Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, who opens the doors of the study house to everyone. Gamliel goes to apologize, and is restored, sharing the post. The story keeps both values in view: respect for leaders and limits on their power.

Historians treat these accounts carefully. They were written down generations later, and some details may be shaped for teaching. But the picture of Yavneh as a working court with a *patriarch*, called the Nasi, at its head matches what later Roman law says about a Jewish patriarch in the Land of Israel.

words.d: head of the sages at Yavneh in about 80–115 CE, remembered as a strong leader who was once removed and then restored
prince or patriarch; the title of the head of the sages in the Land of Israel from Yavneh to the 5th century
the first sliver of the moon each month; the court at Yavneh declared it, fixing the calendar and festival dates

look.title: The Staff and the Purse
look.text: Rabbi Yehoshua works out that Yom Kippur falls on a different day than the court declared. Rabban Gamliel orders him to come on his Yom Kippur carrying a staff and money, things forbidden on that holy day. Rabbi Yehoshua goes. The Gemara (Rosh Hashanah 25a) says Gamliel kissed him on the head and called him his teacher in wisdom and his student in obedience.
look.prompt: Why might a court need its ruling to stand even when a scholar shows it may be wrong? What is lost if it does? What is lost if it does not?

check.q: Why does Rabban Gamliel order Rabbi Yehoshua to come on his Yom Kippur with staff and money?
choices: To show that the court's calendar ruling stands
To pay a fine to Rome
check.why: Rosh Hashanah 25a uses the scene to show that the court's declared date is binding even if a calculation disagrees.

check.q: What happens in Berakhot 27b–28a after Gamliel shames Rabbi Yehoshua too often?
choices: The sages remove Gamliel and appoint Elazar ben Azariah
check.why: The sages remove Gamliel from office; he later apologizes and is restored to share the post.

check.q: What was the Nasi?
choices: The patriarch, head of the sages in the Land of Israel
check.why: Nasi means prince or patriarch, the title of the head of the sages from Yavneh onward.

lessons.title: Bar Kokhba and Rabbi Akiva
lessons.mainIdea: A second revolt, 132–135 CE, ended in defeat, and Rabbi Akiva, who had hoped in its leader, died as one of Rome's martyrs.
reading: Sixty years after the Temple burned, Judea rose again. Its leader was Shimon bar Kosiba, whom followers called *Bar Kokhba*, son of a star. The revolt lasted from 132 to 135 CE under the emperor Hadrian. For a time the rebels held much of Judea and struck their own coins. Then Rome crushed them, and Hadrian renamed the province Syria Palaestina.

The Jerusalem Talmud, in tractate Ta'anit (chapter 4), reports that *Rabbi Akiva* saw Bar Kokhba and applied to him a verse about a star rising from Jacob, calling him the king Messiah. Another sage answered that grass would grow from Akiva's cheeks before the Messiah came. The same passage later calls the leader Bar Koziba, son of a lie. Tradition kept both the hope and the bitterness.

Akiva had come to study late, the Talmud says, after years as a shepherd. By the time of the revolt he was the leading sage of his generation. Rome outlawed teaching Torah. Akiva kept teaching. Berakhot 61b tells that he was arrested and executed, and that as he died he recited the Shema, the declaration that God is one, drawing out the word one until his breath ended.

In 1960 archaeologists led by Yigael Yadin found letters signed by Shimon bar Kosiba in caves in the Judean desert, along with the belongings of rebels who hid there. For historians these letters are rare direct evidence from the revolt. They show a commander giving orders about supplies and festival branches, not the star or the lie of later memory.

words.d: son of a star, the name followers gave Shimon bar Kosiba, leader of the revolt against Rome in 132–135 CE
the leading sage of the early 2nd century CE, who tradition says began study late, hoped in Bar Kokhba, and was executed by Rome
the declaration that God is one, from Deuteronomy 6:4, said morning and evening; Akiva died reciting it

look.title: Star or Lie
look.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai taught: my teacher Akiva would explain the verse, a star goes forth from Jacob, as: Koziba goes forth from Jacob. When Rabbi Akiva saw Bar Koziba he would say: this is the king Messiah. Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta said to him: Akiva, grass will grow from your cheeks and the son of David will still not have come.
look.cite: Jerusalem Talmud, Ta'anit 4:5 (some editions 4:8), paraphrased from the Aramaic and Hebrew
look.prompt: Two sages, one leader, two verdicts. Why might the editors keep Akiva's hope in the text after the revolt failed?

check.q: When was the Bar Kokhba revolt?
check.why: The Bar Kokhba revolt against Hadrian lasted from 132 to 135 CE; 66–70 was the earlier war.

check.q: What did Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta say about Akiva's hope in Bar Kokhba?
choices: Grass will grow from your cheeks before the Messiah comes
Bar Kokhba is a Roman spy
check.why: The Jerusalem Talmud, Ta'anit chapter 4, records his sharp reply to Akiva.

check.q: What did the letters found in 1960 in the Judean desert show?
choices: Bar Kosiba giving orders about supplies and festival branches
check.why: The Bar Kosiba letters are practical commands from the rebel leader, rare direct evidence of the revolt.

lessons.title: Usha, the Galilee and Judah the Prince
lessons.mainIdea: After 135 CE the sages moved north to the Galilee, where Rabbi Judah the Prince gathered the Mishnah in about 200 CE.
reading: Rome's victory in 135 emptied much of Judea of Jews and, for a time, banned teaching. The sages who survived regrouped in the north, in the *Galilee*. Rabbinic tradition names Usha as their first meeting place, then Shefaram, Beit She'arim, Sepphoris and finally Tiberias. Each move is remembered in a list in Rosh Hashanah 31a–b.

The leader of the next generations was *Rabbi Judah the Prince*, called in the Talmud simply Rabbi, or Rabbeinu HaKadosh, our holy teacher. He held the office of Nasi, was wealthy, and, tradition says, was on friendly terms with a Roman ruler the Talmud calls Antoninus. Historians cannot identify that ruler with certainty.

In about 200 CE Judah the Prince completed the *Mishnah*, the collected teachings of the sages from Hillel to his own day, arranged by subject in six orders. It is written in Hebrew, in short, clear statements, and it records minority opinions alongside the majority. Rabbinic tradition holds that he wrote down what had been passed on orally; historians debate how much was already written.

Judah the Prince was buried at Beit She'arim, where archaeologists have uncovered a large Jewish cemetery with carved tombs and inscriptions in Hebrew, Greek and Aramaic. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage site. The Mishnah is the base of both Talmuds. The Gemara of the next three centuries is a conversation about it.

words.d: the hilly northern region of the Land of Israel where the sages settled after 135 CE
the Nasi who compiled the Mishnah in about 200 CE; the Talmud calls him simply Rabbi
the collection of the sages' teachings in six orders, compiled c. 200 CE, on which the Gemara comments

look.title: The Mishnah by the Numbers
look.cite: Standard counts of the Mishnah's structure; date as commonly given by historians
look.prompt: Six orders hold sixty-three tractates. What does that arrangement by subject let a student do that a list of teachers in order would not?

check.q: Where did the sages regroup after the Bar Kokhba revolt?
choices: In the Galilee, at Usha and other towns
check.why: Rosh Hashanah 31a–b lists the moves of the court northward through the Galilee, starting at Usha.

check.q: What did Rabbi Judah the Prince complete in about 200 CE?
check.why: Judah the Prince compiled the Mishnah, the base text of both Talmuds, in about 200 CE.

check.q: In what language is the Mishnah written?
check.why: The Mishnah is in Hebrew; the Gemara that discusses it is mostly in Aramaic.

lessons.title: Reading the Sources Side by Side
lessons.mainIdea: Historians build the story of this period from Josephus, Roman writers, coins and ruins, and read the Talmud's stories as teaching written down later.
reading: Two kinds of *sources* tell us about the years from 63 BCE to 200 CE. The first were written at the time or close to it: Josephus, Roman historians like Tacitus, the New Testament, inscriptions and coins. The second is the rabbinic literature, the Mishnah and the two Talmuds, whose stories about this period were written down between 200 and 600 CE.

Historians ask of any story: who told it, when, and why? A rabbi's story recorded four hundred years after the event may preserve true memory. It may also be shaped to teach a lesson, such as the danger of shaming a guest. The coffin story about Yochanan ben Zakkai appears in several versions, and each version tells the request a little differently. That is a sign, historians say, of a story that grew in the telling.

*Archaeology* gives evidence no one wrote for us. The Arch of Titus confirms the Temple's treasures were carried to Rome. Bar Kokhba's coins, stamped with the words for the freedom of Israel, confirm his rebels ran a government. The tombs at Beit She'arim confirm a wealthy, Greek-speaking Jewish community around the Nasi.

The Talmud and the historians do not compete. They answer different questions. Historians ask what happened. The Talmud asks what it means and what a Jew should do about it. A good student of this period keeps both questions open and says which one a given text is answering.

words.d: any text, object or record that tells about the past; historians ask who made it, when and why
the study of the past through things dug up: buildings, coins, tombs and written scraps

look.title: Which Question Is It Answering?
look.text: Item A: a bronze coin from 133 CE reading, in Hebrew letters, Year two of the freedom of Israel. Item B: the Gemara in Gittin 56a saying that Vespasian offered Yochanan ben Zakkai any request. Item C: Josephus's count of the dead at Jerusalem, which most historians think is far too high. Item D: the story of Akiva dying while reciting the Shema, in Berakhot 61b.
look.prompt: For each item, say whether it mainly answers what happened or what it means. Which item would you trust most for a date, and which for a value?

check.q: Which of these is a source written at the time of the events?
check.why: Josephus wrote in the 1st century CE, close to the events; the rabbinic works were written down centuries later.

check.q: What do Bar Kokhba's coins confirm for historians?
choices: That the rebels ran a government
check.why: Coins stamped with the freedom of Israel show the rebels minted money, a sign of a working government.

check.q: Why do historians read the Talmud's stories about 70 CE with care?
choices: They were written down centuries later and shaped to teach
check.why: Rabbinic stories about this period were recorded between 200 and 600 CE and often carry a lesson, so historians weigh them against earlier sources.

lessons.title: From Temple to Study House
lessons.mainIdea: Between 70 and 200 CE Judaism shifted its center from the Temple and its priests to the study house and its sages, and the Mishnah is the record of that shift.
reading: Look at the beginning and the end of this chapter. In 63 BCE the center of Jewish life was a building, the Temple, and the men who served in it, the *priests*. In 200 CE the center was a book, the Mishnah, and the men who studied it, the sages. No emperor ordered that change. It happened one ruling and one school at a time.

Historians name three steps. First, the Pharisees had already taught that Torah could be studied and practiced anywhere, not only through the Temple. Second, Yavneh gave those teachers a court and a calendar. Third, the Galilee gave them a generation of peace under Judah the Prince, long enough to write it all down.

The Mishnah itself shows the shift. Whole orders deal with Temple offerings and purity, described in the present tense as if the Temple still stood. Rabbinic tradition holds that study of those laws keeps them alive until, in Jewish hope, the Temple is rebuilt. Other tractates deal with blessings, courts, damages and marriage, the daily life of a people without a Temple.

The next chapter follows the sages who read the Mishnah for three hundred more years, in the Galilee and in Babylon. Their conversation is the *Gemara*. Mishnah and Gemara together are the Talmud. Everything the Talmud says about Hillel, Yochanan and Akiva reaches us through that conversation.

words.d: the kohanim, descendants of Aaron, who served in the Temple; their role shrank after 70 CE
the discussion of the Mishnah by the sages of c. 200–500 CE, mostly in Aramaic; with the Mishnah it forms the Talmud

look.title: Before and After
look.text: Before 70 CE: a Jew in Judea brings a lamb to Jerusalem at Passover, a priest offers it, and the family eats it that night in the city. After 70 CE: a Jew in the Galilee, or in Babylon, sits at a table at home, tells the story of the Exodus from a set text, eats unleavened bread and bitter herbs, and says blessings the sages arranged. The Mishnah, tractate Pesachim chapter 10, describes that home meal.
look.prompt: What stayed the same between the two scenes? What replaced what? Who leads in each one?

check.q: What replaced the Temple as the center of Jewish life by 200 CE, according to historians?
choices: The study house and the sages' book, the Mishnah
check.why: The chapter traces the shift from Temple and priests to study house and sages, recorded in the Mishnah.

check.q: Why does the Mishnah describe Temple offerings in the present tense?
choices: The Temple still stood in 200 CE
Rabbinic tradition holds that studying the laws keeps them alive
The sages forgot the Temple had fallen
check.why: The Temple fell in 70 CE; the sages studied its laws as a way of keeping them, in hope of a rebuilt Temple.

check.q: What are Mishnah and Gemara together called?
check.why: The Mishnah plus the Gemara that discusses it equals the Talmud.

choices: Alexander the Great arrives in the region
review.why: Alexander came in 332 BCE, Pompey in 63 BCE, the Temple burned in 70 CE, and the Mishnah was completed c. 200 CE.

review.q: Which group did the Sadducees reject?
review.why: Josephus says the Sadducees accepted the written Torah but not the Pharisees' added traditions.

review.q: What does Eruvin 13b say about the two houses of Hillel and Shammai?
choices: Both are the words of the living God, but the law follows Hillel
review.why: The Gemara reports a heavenly voice honoring both views while ruling like the House of Hillel.
Josephus, a Jewish general who went over to Rome, wrote the fullest account of the war of 66–70 CE.

review.q: What did Yochanan ben Zakkai ask of Vespasian?
review.why: Gittin 56b gives his request: Yavneh and its sages, Gamliel's family, and a doctor for Rabbi Tzadok.

review.q: Which verse does Avot de-Rabbi Natan attach to acts of loving-kindness after the Temple's fall?
choices: Hosea 6:6, I desire mercy, and not sacrifice
Psalm 137, by the rivers of Babylon
review.why: Yochanan quotes Hosea 6:6 to say kindness can serve as atonement.

review.q: What did Hadrian do after defeating Bar Kokhba?
review.why: After 135 CE Hadrian renamed Judea Syria Palaestina; teaching was banned for a time and the sages moved to the Galilee.

review.q: Which text was written down closest to the events it describes?
choices: The Jerusalem Talmud on Bar Kokhba
Bar Kosiba's own letters found in 1960
review.why: The letters were written during the revolt itself; the rabbinic texts were compiled centuries later.
